cues.text: A Woman Healed and Transformed

Mary Magdalene takes her name from Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, and the Gospel of Luke introduces her among a group of women who accompanied Jesus and the Twelve, and who supported them out of their own resources — a detail that reveals both her material means and her deep personal gratitude, since Luke tells us plainly that Jesus had cast out of her seven demons, a severe affliction from which she had evidently been dramatically and completely delivered.

From the moment of that healing forward, Mary appears consistently among Jesus's most devoted followers — not one of the Twelve, but part of a wider circle of women disciples whose faithful presence the Gospels take care to record even when the male disciples' own courage occasionally faltered.
A Circle of Women Who Never Left

Luke names Mary Magdalene alongside Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza, and Susanna, among "many others" who provided for Jesus and the Twelve out of their own resources — a detail easy to pass over quickly, but one that reveals a genuine community of women disciples supporting Christ's public ministry financially and practically from very early on, a partnership the Gospels take pains to record even though the culture of the day rarely gave women's contributions such deliberate attention.
Present When Others Fled

All four Gospels place Mary Magdalene at the foot of the cross during the Crucifixion, standing alongside the Mother of Jesus and the beloved disciple while most of the male followers, by their own later admission, had scattered in fear for their own safety.

This same faithful presence carried her, along with several other women, to Jesus's tomb early on the third day, bringing spices to properly anoint a body that Jewish burial custom, interrupted by the onset of the Sabbath, had not yet allowed them time to prepare — an act of simple, grieving devotion that would place her, by God's providence, at the very center of the most important event in human history.
The First Witness of the Resurrection

Finding the tomb empty and the stone rolled away, Mary Magdalene, according to John's Gospel, remained weeping outside even after the other women and disciples had gone, until a figure she at first mistook for the gardener spoke her name — Mary — and she recognized, in that single spoken word, the voice of the Risen Christ himself.

Jesus's instruction to her was direct and unmistakable: go to my brothers and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God — commissioning this one faithful, grieving woman, before any of the Apostles had yet encountered the risen Lord, to be the very first herald of the Resurrection.
"Apostle to the Apostles"

Mary Magdalene's obedience to this commission — running to tell Peter and the other disciples, I have seen the Lord — earned her, from ancient times, the title Apostola Apostolorum , "Apostle to the Apostles," a designation used already by early Church writers and later given renewed emphasis by St.

Thomas Aquinas : the recognition that the first person entrusted to proclaim the central message of the entire Christian faith was not one of the Twelve, but this one faithful woman who had simply refused to leave the tomb.
A Reputation Long Misunderstood

For many centuries in the Western Church, Mary Magdalene was popularly conflated with the unnamed sinful woman who anoints Jesus's feet in Luke's Gospel and with Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus — an identification modern biblical scholarship has largely set aside, since the Gospel texts themselves do not clearly support treating these as the same woman.

Whatever the truth of these separate identifications, the genuine, textually secure Mary Magdalene of the Gospels needs no borrowed story to establish her greatness: a woman healed by Christ, faithful at the cross when others fled, and the first witness of his rising.
Legacy

In 2016, recognizing the singular dignity of her witness, Pope Francis elevated Mary Magdalene's liturgical celebration to the rank of a Feast, placing her, in the Church's calendar, on the same level of solemnity long accorded to the male Apostles — a decree explicitly framed by the Congregation for Divine Worship as an invitation to reflect more deeply on the dignity of women and on the greatness of the mystery of divine mercy.

She remains a permanent, luminous reminder that the Gospel entrusts its central proclamation not only to the mighty or the officially credentialed, but to whoever, healed by Christ's own mercy, is faithful enough to remain present at the foot of the cross and at the door of the empty tomb.
